newsitem.title: RUSSIA: YELTSIN SAYS ROUBLE REFORM WILL TAKE NO VICTIMS.
newsitem.headline: YELTSIN SAYS ROUBLE REFORM WILL TAKE NO VICTIMS.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, explaining plans to lop three zeroes off the rouble, assured Russians on Friday the currency reform would not make anyone suffer.
The reform plans confirmed Russia had defeated inflation and would restore confidence in the rouble, he said.

"Of course previous reforms, starting from 1947, always took something from citizens...As a result there was panic, stress, people crushed in lines and always victims," Yeltsin said in a regular nationwide radio address.

"Nothing like that will happen now. The currency reform which we have announced will not lead to any confiscation (of money). Therefore we announced it in advance. I want there to be no rushing, no panic this time."
Yeltsin announced on Monday that the rouble would be redenominated from the start of next year, meaning one new rouble will equal 1,000 old ones.

The Central Bank said the era of hyperinflation and economic stagnation was over. To avoid the panic caused by earlier reforms which forced Russians to trade in old notes quickly, it said old notes would be exchanged for new ones until 2002.
Yeltsin, 66, celebrated what he said would be the return to a "normal" currency and said he foresaw no more major depreciations in the value of the rouble.
"With this currency reform we declare firmly that we have conquered inflation. We have it firmly under control," he said.
"I am convinced there will come a time when Russians are proud of their rouble and we will not change it for any dollar."
Inflation has slowed sharply over the last couple of years from year-on-year rates of more than 1,000 percent in 1993 in the early stages of Russia's market reforms.
The year-on-year rate in June was 14.5 percent but prices in some shops are still marked in dollars.
Yeltsin said savings and bank deposits would not be devalued and that knocking three zeroes off the rouble would make shopping and working out the household budget easier.
"There is no need to worry -- there will be no leap in prices. Nothing will disappear from the shops. There will be no victims of reforms," he said.
"Many people do not go in to a shop today without a calculator. That is understandable...It has come to the point where going to a shop often turns into an arithmetics test."
